buyer_reported_costs.finding: A nonprofit program director says the next human answering option was $400 a month.

buyer_reported_costs.context: Vendor-published ROI case study for Fortify's 'Lucy' AI receptionist; cost is for five locations combined, so it is not a single-location list price

buyer_reported_costs.finding: One user reported being asked nearly $60 a month just to keep access to calls/voicemail after a free-tier change; another reported waiting nine months for a promised refund.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Third-party analysis of 55 user reports (Reddit, Trustpilot, App Store) about AI receptionists; reported complaints, not verified invoices

buyer_reported_costs.finding: A managed IT provider says one client cut call handling from $4,500 a month with a human receptionist service to under $500 a month with an AI receptionist.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Vendor case study by Seashore IT (Western US, not New Jersey); the $500 figure is a client total, not a published list price

buyer_reported_costs.finding: A vendor comparison states that a live answering service runs about $1.50 to $1.90 a minute, versus roughly 13¢ a minute on its own Starter plan at four-minute calls.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Goodcall's own pricing FAQ; vendor marketing claim used as an anchor for human-answering cost, not an invoice or independent benchmark

what_is_included_vs_extra.point: Smith.ai bundles human escalation into its AI-first plan: if something complex comes up the call can be transferred to a live North America-based receptionist any time, day or night, per the vendor's FAQ.

Goodcall does not meter minutes at all — a 30-second wrong number and a nine-minute booking cost nothing extra — but what the client gets is an AI agent with transfers to people the client chooses ('choose who receives transfers'), and the pricing page does not describe a human receptionist backup.

Calendar booking and warm/live transfers are not on Rosie's $49 entry plan, which sends appointment links by text; booking directly on the calendar and warm transfers start on the $149 plan, so a usable booking receptionist costs three times the headline price.

Dialzara bills phone numbers separately ($3/month US and Canada local, $5/month US toll-free), plus $19/month + $0.05 per AI message for SMS (carrier fees $0.0083 per segment) and $39/month standalone for website chat, which is free with voice plans at 100 sessions/month; custom prompted/engineered setup is only included on Elite or the $1,500+ Done for You! tier.

Rosie's entry plan covers 250 minutes for $49 while the $149 plan covers 1,000 and the $299 plan 2,000, so the effective price per included minute falls sharply with tier; a website texting add-on is $50/month for 25 conversations plus $1 per additional conversation.

Upfirst includes CRM API/Zapier and calendar booking on every plan, but team-done integration setup, white-glove onboarding and priority support only on Scale/Enterprise; each extra agent costs $9.95/month.
Goodcall's tiers limit external tools (1/5/15), team members (1/5/10), workers (5/20) and AI test runs; test-run top-ups cost $5 at a time and Starter keeps only 30 days of call history.

My AI Front Desk includes 200 voice minutes and a 1,000-credit overage pool (25 credits = $0.25 per voice minute, about 40 extra minutes) that resets each billing cycle; auto-reload adds 1,000 credits for $10 and those purchased credits never expire, rolling over month to month.

Sarah 24/7 includes white-glove setup, porting, calendar/CRM connections, after-hours and Spanish at no extra charge, and charges the same 35¢/minute with no penalty tier; a second channel is $100/month.

Fusion Calling includes all integrations even on Starter, but adds one-time setup of $799 on Pro and $1,250 on Enterprise for configuration, integration setup, testing and launch support; its annual billing toggle is labelled 'Save 10%' and overage rates rise as tiers shrink ($0.30 / $0.25 / $0.20 per minute).
ZAVYANS quotes a management retainer but bills AI platform usage (call minutes/messages) separately at cost, so the advertised monthly price is not the all-in cost.
Lithium's $179 managed plan includes setup, call rules, calendar/CRM hooks and testing, but publishes no minute allowance or overage rate, so usage risk is undisclosed.

Slang.ai bundles reservation-platform integrations, bilingual support and white glove support at Core, but custom workflows, custom integrations, reporting/dashboards and SSO/access controls only at Enterprise.

buyer_complaints.complaint: Callers hang up on the AI and the business never finds out; because no message or transcript is created, the lost lead leaves no trace.
Agents loop, repeat themselves or misunderstand accents and off-script requests instead of handing off to a person.
Usage-based billing surprises: short calls billed like long ones, credit tiers, and unclear overage rules are the most common pricing complaints.
Booking errors, including wrong service booked or double-booked jobs, create more work than the AI saves.
The sales demo is smoother than the real deployment, and some buyers report aggressive upsell pitches during onboarding.
Per-call billing irritates some law-firm buyers, who describe it as sketchy or steep at $7-$9 per call; they prefer predictable billing.

price_ranges.low_cost_self_serve: $0-$99/month entry plans; allowances vary widely across the band — 25 calls (Smith.ai Free), 30 calls (Upfirst Starter $24.95), 60 minutes (Dialzara Lite $29), 90 calls (Upfirst Premium $59.95), 100 unique customers (Goodcall Starter $79), 200 minutes (My AI Front Desk $99) and 250 minutes (Rosie Professional $49)
price_ranges.mid_market: $99-$349/month; published plans are $99 (My AI Front Desk, Dialzara Pro), $149 (Rosie Scale, Fusion Calling Starter), $150 (Smith.ai Pro), $159.95 (Upfirst Pro), $179 (Lithium), $199 (Dialzara Plus), $299 (Rosie Growth, Goodcall Scale, Upfirst Scale, UpNewLevel Basic) and $349 (Dialzara Elite), with allowances from 75 calls to 2,000 minutes or 2,000 unique customers
price_ranges.full_service_or_custom: $350-$1,500+/month, plus $499-$1,999 one-time setup at managed vendors: Sarah 24/7 from $350/month plus $0.35/min, Slang.ai from $399/$599 per location, Fusion Calling Enterprise $497/month plus $1,250 setup, Smith.ai Enterprise $500/month, UpNewLevel Pro $599/month, ZAVYANS $249-$799/month plus $499-$1,999 setup, Dialzara Done for You! from $1,500+/month
price_ranges.inference_note: Ranges are the low and high published list prices observed on the vendor pages on 2026-11-12, grouped by price band, not averages or quotes. Entry plans sit at or under $99 and their allowances vary widely (25 calls to 250 minutes). Plans priced $99-$349 are where booking, warm transfers or a larger minute/customer allowance appear. Managed or done-for-you offers with setup, tuning and (at some vendors) human escalation start at $350 and run to $1,500+, with one-time setup of $499-$1,999 observed only at ZAVYANS ($499/$999/$1,999) and Fusion Calling ($799/$1,250). Usage overages and add-ons (phone numbers, SMS, extra agents, extra channels, website texting) sit on top and are excluded from the ranges.

implications_for_consultancy: Inference: the consultancy should compete in the roughly $149-$599/month managed band rather than the $29-$99 self-serve band. Reasoning: the local/tri-state managed offers in this set publish $179 (Lithium), $299 and $599 (UpNewLevel) and from $350 plus $0.35/minute (Sarah 24/7), and ZAVYANS runs $249-$799; self-serve tools at $29-$99 leave the buyer to write prompts, wire calendars and design escalation. A consultancy's labour is the product, so it should be priced against managed providers, not software seats.

Inference: a one-time setup fee inside the $499-$1,999 band is defensible because managed vendors already publish fees in that band. Reasoning: ZAVYANS publishes $499/$999/$1,999 one-off setup and Fusion Calling publishes $799 (Pro) and $1,250 (Enterprise) one-time setup, both describing it as agent configuration, integration setup, testing and launch support. Charging $0 setup would undervalue work buyers already pay for.

Inference: the strongest recurring price points are roughly $249-$349 for a single-location 5-20 staff client and $449-$799 for multi-location or CRM-heavy clients. Reasoning: these bracket published managed plans (Lithium $179, ZAVYANS $249-$799, UpNewLevel $299, Sarah 24/7 $350, Smith.ai Enterprise $500) while staying below the $1,000-$2,500 some buyers report paying human answering services.

Inference: a pilot priced around $500-$1,500 including setup, 30 days of tuning and a written escalation plan is likely to convert, because it is smaller than a year of $299-$599 monthly fees and sits at the low end of observed one-time setup fees. Reasoning: buyers' most-reported fears are billing surprises and demo-vs-reality gaps, so a fixed-scope paid pilot answers that objection directly.

Inference: include human escalation, after-hours rules, bilingual handling and transcript review in the base retainer rather than selling them as add-ons. Reasoning: Smith.ai charges for its human backup inside the plan and Sarah 24/7 bundles Spanish and after-hours, while buyer reports focus on hangups, loops and missed handoffs — the failures a cheap self-serve deployment leaves with the client.

Inference: avoid per-call pricing and publish a clear included-minute allowance with a capped overage. Reasoning: per-call billing draws complaints from law-firm buyers, usage/credit billing is the most common pricing complaint in the 55-report analysis, and several vendors worsen the risk by not publishing an allowance at all (Lithium, UpNewLevel, Slang.ai), which a consultancy can beat by being explicit.

Inference: the margin should come from configuration and ongoing tuning, not from reselling minutes. Reasoning: software costs are publicly visible ($29-$349/month with $0.20-$0.48/min overage; white-label or partner programs at Dialzara and Fusion Calling), so clients can benchmark the software component; integration, testing, call review and accountability are what a local firm can charge for.

Inference: offer annual prepay at roughly 10-17% off rather than matching '2 months free' across the board. Reasoning: Rosie advertises 'Pay Annually, 2 months free' (about 17%), Fusion Calling's annual toggle is labelled 'Save 10%', and My AI Front Desk prices annual at $79/mo versus $99/mo (about 20%) — the observed band runs 10-20%, and a practice with heavy first-year labour should sit at the low end.

Inference: a retainer that bundles roughly 200-300 voice minutes of usage with tuning can be priced at $249-$349 without looking expensive. Reasoning: $99 already buys 200-220 minutes at My AI Front Desk and Dialzara Pro, and $149 buys 500 minutes at Fusion Calling and 1,000 at Rosie Scale, so the usage inside a $249-$349 retainer is cheap for the consultancy to fund while the visible market comparison stays favourable.
caveats: All vendor list prices were read on 2026-11-12. Prices on these pages change frequently and several render tiers by script, so a later visit may differ.

Smith.ai prints $150/mo at $2.00/call for 75 calls and $500/mo at $1.67/call for 300 calls on Enterprise. The 150-call and 300-call totals inside the Pro selector are shown only as per-call rates ($1.80 with '-10%' and $1.67 with '-17%'); the corresponding monthly totals (~$270 and ~$500) are arithmetic, not printed, and are labelled as such.
Rosie's page renders the plan labels out of price order (Professional $49, Scale $149, Growth $299). Tier names are reported as the vendor shows them; buyers should confirm at checkout.

Rosie publishes no voice overage rate in retrievable text: the 'What happens if I go over my minutes?' FAQ is collapsed and its answer did not render, so overage handling is recorded as not stated rather than inferred.

Goodcall's live pricing page (2026-11-12) shows $79/$129/$299 for 100/500/2,000 unique customers with 79¢/26¢/15¢ overage; it publishes no annual prices and no cancellation mechanics, so those are recorded as not stated.

Slang.ai's $399 and $599 figures appear in the page markup as USD 'Starting at ... *per location'; the same page also contains CAD and AUD variants ($399 CAD, AUD $399) and switches by visitor region, so only the USD figures are used. Every plan routes to a 'Get a quote' form.

Several vendors do not publish usage allowances, overage rates, setup fees or contract lengths (Lithium, UpNewLevel, Slang.ai), and others do not publish annual totals (Rosie, Goodcall). 'Not published' is recorded rather than estimated.

My AI Front Desk's allowance and credit mechanics come from the vendor's own billing tutorial rather than the pricing page alone; the tutorial also describes a $0/mo Free plan that is not listed as a tier here.

Buyer-reported figures are anecdotes or vendor case studies, not audited invoices. Case-study costs may cover multiple locations and are labeled as such, and the $1.50-$1.90/minute human-answering comparison is the vendor's own claim.

G2, Capterra and Trustpilot blocked automated access during this research, so review evidence is drawn from accessible third-party analyses, forums and vendor pages rather than the review sites' full text.

Numa (the dealership AI phone agent named in the brief) publishes no price; its FAQ says plans are scaled to team size and systems and priced after a demo. It is therefore excluded from the offerings list and noted in data_gaps.
data_gaps: Numa: no public price. Vendor FAQ says plans are scaled to team size and systems and priced after a demo; a third-party estimate of about $199/month per location is unconfirmed and was not used.
Smith.ai does not print monthly totals for its 150-call and 300-call Pro selector options, its 500-call Enterprise option or its 1,000+ custom option; only per-call rates are shown.
Rosie's exact annual-billing totals (as opposed to '2 months free') are not displayed, and its overage/minutes FAQ answer did not render.
